instantiated_cells.justification: The statute defines 'lobbying' as attempting to influence legislative or administrative action by oral or written communication and expressly includes time spent preparing for such communication and appearances at public hearings/meetings or service on a committee where such preparation/communication occurs.

A 'lobbyist' is any individual employed by or receiving economic consideration from a principal whose duties include lobbying (including employees of principals when they meet the 5-day test), and lobbying as a lobbyist is restricted to licensed/authorized persons, which covers both outside professionals and in-house employees who lobby.
The definitions section lists multiple defined terms but does not define 'public entity' or a comparable general term.

Coverage hinges on monetary thresholds—principals register only after exceeding $500 in lobbying expenditures/obligations, and principals anticipating not more than $500 may file a verified statement and be exempt from licensing/registration/reporting if true.

Lobbying includes communications with 'any elective state official' and legislative action includes actions of the governor in approving/vetoing bills, so the definition covers communications with legislators and executive officials including the governor.

Lobbying targets are defined as communications with elective state officials, agency officials, and legislative employees, covering both legislative and executive/administrative branch decision-makers and relevant staff.

Because lobbying is oral/written communication with elective state officials and legislative action includes the governor's bill approval/veto, communications with both legislators and the governor are included.
The definition of lobbying includes communications with 'any elective state official,' which by definition includes persons holding elective state office (including the governor and legislators).

A 'lobbying communication' is any oral or written communication with an agency official, elective state official, or legislative employee that attempts to influence legislative or administrative action, confirming the same broad target set.

Lobbying is directed to elective state officials (legislative/executive), agency officials (administrative), and legislative employees, which captures legislative and executive/administrative targets including staff.

The registration/licensure scheme applies to individuals lobbying for economic consideration as 'lobbyists,' while elective state officials and legislative employees acting in an official capacity are expressly not subject to key lobbying provisions.

The definition of 'lobbyist' includes individuals employed by a principal (i.e., in-house/public employees when employed by a principal) and applies a time standard (lobbying communications on at least 5 days in a reporting period) when duties are not exclusively lobbying, with compensation defined as economic consideration other than expense reimbursement.

Neither the definitions of 'agency' nor 'principal' rely on a public charter or special governmental protection as a criterion; they define governmental units and principals by role rather than charter status.
No definition in the provided text defines covered entities based on ownership (e.g., state ownership or private ownership percentage).
The statute's definitions do not classify entities by revenue structure or composition as a basis for coverage.
